newsitem.title: USA: Senate action on federal money bills stalls.
newsitem.headline: Senate action on federal money bills stalls.

text.p: Senate Republicans Tuesday abruptly withdrew yet another spending bill after Democrats tried to attach politically charged amendments, adding pressure for a quick budget deal with the White House.

Senate Majority Leader Trent Lott, a Republican from Mississippi, remained upbeat and said his decision to withdraw the Interior Department appropriations bill meant most of the government's activities would be paid for out of a massive appropriations bill to be negotiated with President Clinton.

Democrats had tried to offer a $3.1 billion increase in federal funding for education, but were blocked by Republican leaders. They had also signalled other amendments opposed by Republicans would be brought up for debate.
"Maybe we have reached a point where they are not going to agree to do it without their political games," Lott told reporters just before he ended debate on the bill.
Lott also said he had threatened to meet Democrats one-for-one with amendments aimed at currying favour with voters just before the November election.
"If you are just going to play political games, show me yours and I'll show you mine. For every political amendment they offer, we will offer one," he said.

Last Friday, Lott suddenly halted debate on the Treasury Department's appropriation when Democrats said they would demand a vote on their plan to rein in restrictive rules set by health plans on communications between doctors and patients. Republican leaders said the health issue needed full hearings and was unrelated to the funding bill.

Earlier Tuesday, Republican senators had announced they would support a $2.3 billion increase in education funding to be paid for with the anticipated $2 billion proceeds from the sale of radio airwaves and cuts in domestic programmes.

A principal sponsor of the Democratic education plan, Sen. Edward Kennedy of Massachusetts, said the Republican offer represented a major concession. However, he accused them of a pre-election conversion to support education. Echoing this, Sen. Tom Harkin, a Democrat from Iowa, told reporters: "Now they want to play catch-up ball. It really is a cynical ploy."
Before they can hit the campaign trail full time, Congress must assure their principal work -- the funding of government activities -- is completed.

Clinton has signed four of the 13 must-pass appropriations bills needed to keep the government running after the Oct. 1 start of the new fiscal year. One more, the energy and water projects bill, cleared Congress Tuesday.

Contentious negotiations are expected as they struggle to resolve disputes over the remaining eight, most of which are expected to be wrapped into one massive spending bill to be considered by next week.

White House Chief of Staff Leon Panetta started the talks with Congress last night as he came to the Capitol to seek a $6.5 billion boost in domestic spending paid for with cuts in defence programmes.

Meanwhile, a House-Senate Appropriations Conference Committee reached tentative agreement Tuesday to spend $12.1 billion on foreign aid in 1997, virtually the same as 1996 but $800 million below the White House request.
The committee failed to resolve a dispute over a House plan to tie assistance to international family planning groups to their position on abortion.
